title: What Is a Trade Credit? How B2B Trade Credits Work
summary: A trade credit allows you to buy goods from a supplier and pay at a later date—or vice versa. Favorable trade credit terms can help improve your cash flow.
body_text: This post is for information only. You are responsible for reviewing and using this information appropriately. This content doesn’t contain and isn’t meant to provide legal, tax, or business advice. Requirements are updated frequently and you should make sure to do your own research and reach out to professional legal, tax, and business advisers, as needed. To sell products using the Shopify platform, you must comply with the laws of the jurisdiction of your business and your customers, the Shopify Terms of Service, the Shopify Acceptable Use Policy, and any other applicable policies. Trade credit is a business-to-business (B2B) arrangement that lets a buyer purchase goods or services from a supplier and pay at a later date. This arrangement functions as an interest-free loan for the buyer, while for sellers it offers an incentive to customers that helps build strong relationships. Access to flexible, short-term financing is critical for small businesses struggling with cash flow . According to the Federal Reserve’s 2026 Small Business Credit Survey , 60% of small employers had applied for financing in the past year, with 56% of those applicants seeking funds to meet standard operating expenses . Because traditional lenders often deny or only partially fund loan applications, establishing direct financing terms between trade partners helps to bridge this gap. Learn how trade credit works for both buyers and sellers, and how to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of this financing method. You will also learn how to use Shopify B2B tools to extend credit and collect trade credit payments. What is trade credit? Trade credit is a commercial lending relationship between two businesses that bypasses a traditional bank. In business-to-business commerce , a seller lets a buyer take delivery of goods or services with an agreed upon date for payment in the future. This period is known as the credit period, which typically spans 30, 60, or 90 days. Because there’s no financial institution acting as an intermediary, trade credit is often an informal agreement, though larger transactions frequently use a formal agreement or a signed promissory note to legally protect the seller. When a buyer is using trade credit, they effectively obtain an interest-free loan, helping to improve cash flow. Instead of paying for inventory upon ordering, the business retains that capital. It can then sell the finished products to customers, collect the revenue, and use the funds to pay off the supplier invoice on or before the due date. This cycle minimizes the need for outside commercial financing, keeping the business’s debt in check. A business typically resorts to using trade credit during periods of rapid expansion or seasonal demand shifts. When demand spikes, ordering larger quantities requires significant upfront capital. Startups and mid-sized brands use trade credit when their accounts payable volume grows to a point where upfront cash payments strain daily operations. It is also an option when a company has established a consistent payment history and wants to leverage that credibility into extended payment terms to conserve cash. Connect with manufacturers Use this free email template to introduce your business to manufacturers, suppliers, and distributors to source the perfect products for your business. Download template Trade credit vs. other types of financing Trade credit differs from commercial loans, business credit cards, and lines of credit in the following ways: Traditional bank loans. A bank loan provides a lump sum of cash that incurs interest charges from day one, typically requiring monthly payments. Trade credit does not give you cash but rather inventory or materials with a deferred payment window, incurring zero interest if the debt is paid by the due date. Business credit cards. Business credit cards offer short-term funding but have high interest rates if you carry a balance, along with transaction fees for the vendor. Trade credit provides customized terms for the buyer and can reduce or avoid credit card processing fees for the seller if invoices are settled via bank transfer or check. Lines of credit. A business line of credit is a revolving loan from a bank. It requires extensive bank underwriting, regular maintenance fees, and audits of your financial statements. Trade credit is easier to secure because the supplier evaluates your payment history and credit history without involving a bank. Feature Trade Credit Traditional credit Traditional bank loan Lines of credit Source Supplier/vendor Commercial bank Credit card issuer Commercial bank Cost Free (if paid on time) Interest charges Interest + annual fees Maintenance fees Form Goods or services Cash lump sum Revolving credit line Established credit line Approval Vendor evaluation Bank underwriting Personal/business credit check Bank underwriting How trade credit works for buyers and sellers To make trade credit work smoothly, both parties must understand their specific responsibilities, operational workflows, and potential financial risks. How trade credit works for the buyer From the buyer’s side, the process begins when you establish a relationship with a vendor. You submit a commercial credit application detailing your business history, trade references, and financial statements. The supplier evaluates the buyer’s credit profile, checking credit reports through bureaus such as Dun & Bradstreet to review the buyer’s credit rating. Once approved, the supplier grants you a specific credit limit. You can then issue a purchase order without sending immediate payment. Items arrive with an invoice stating the trade credit terms. Your accounting team logs this under accounts payable, tracking the deadline to ensure timely payments and avoid late payments that could damage your credit history. How trade credit works for the seller For the seller, extending trade credit is a tool to increase order sizes and cultivate customer loyalty. When you offer terms, you act as the lender. However, trade credit introduces the risk of delayed revenue and bad debt. A strict credit management process involves reviewing the credit ratings of every business customer before fulfilling orders. Once you ship the goods, the transaction moves into accounts receivable. If a buyer makes late payments or defaults, your cash flow suffers. This poses one of the disadvantages of trade credit if you end up spending time and money chasing payment. Common trade credit payment terms The payment terms dictate when payment is due and whether there are any incentives for early payment. Typical terms include: Net 7, 15, 30, 60, 90. The number represents how many days the buyer has to pay the full invoice amount from the invoice date. For example, net 30 means that payment is due within 30 days. Cash on delivery (COD). Cash on delivery means that the buyer pays the full amount when the goods are delivered rather than ordered. This is common when a buyer has a poor credit history or is working with a supplier for the first time. Payment in advance/upfront payment . The buyer must make upfront payment before the supplier begins production or ships the items. This carries no risk for the seller but can strain the buyer’s cash on hand. Early payment discounts. An early payment discount is a notation that indicates the buyer will receive a discount if they pay within a specified number of days. For example, 2/10 net 30 means the seller offers a 2% discount if the buyer pays within 10 days, which incentivizes buyers to pay earlier, helping the seller manage cash flow. Shopify B2B payment terms Shopify B2B streamlines how sellers manage payment terms by automating various options. Within the Shopify admin, you can configure custom terms for specific business customers, including net 7, 15, 30, 45, 60, or 90 days. Set invoices to become due upon order fulfillment, assign a fixed calendar date, or mandate partial deposit requirements before processing an order. For buyers, tracking inbound inventory requires organized documentation. Use purchase orders to clearly define the agreed-upon trade credit terms (such as net 30 or COD) with your suppliers. Documenting these terms in your procurement system links your order details to your accounting software. This data feeds into your cash flow forecasting tools, giving your finance team visibility into future payment dates so they can reserve capital and avoid unexpected shortfalls. How sellers collect trade credit payments Sellers use several methods to process trade credit payments: Vaulted cards. The buyer puts a credit card on file before or during checkout. The seller automatically charges the card once the net terms deadline is reached. ACH and bank transfers. Automated clearing house (ACH) direct deposits move money electronically from the buyer’s bank account to the seller’s account, processing transactions in batches rather than individually. This cuts overhead, letting banks charge flat, nominal fees instead of the percentage-based fees required by credit card networks. Manual payment. The buyer initiates a wire transfer, sends a physical check, or makes a payment from an online bank account when the invoice comes due. Shopify B2B payment methods To collect balances when trade credit terms come due, Shopify B2B supports multiple flexible payment options. Buyers can store vaulted credit cards or vaulted bank accounts during their initial checkout. When the due date arrives, Shopify automatically processes the payment using the stored account information. Alternatively, you can permit manual payment methods, letting buyers settle trade credit balances outstanding via external ACH transfers, corporate wires, or checks, while Shopify’s systems automatically update your ledger. Try Shopify for free Create a store and bring your idea to life with a free trial. Discover how Shopify helps you manage your business and make sales. Start free trial Best practices for managing trade credit For buyers: Negotiate payment terms that fit your cash cycle For buyers and sellers: Use automated tracking for due dates For sellers: Establish a strict credit policy and stick to it Implementing these best practices for managing trade credit protects your business from cash crunches, whether you are buying supplies or selling finished products. For buyers: Negotiate payment terms that fit your cash cycle Aim to align revenue with expenses. If it takes your business an average of 45 days to convert raw inventory into customer cash, you might negotiate net 60 terms with your suppliers. This buffer allows you to collect revenue from your own sales before you have to pay for the materials, maintaining a positive cash balance. For buyers and sellers: Use automated tracking for due dates Use automated accounting tools or Shopify’s integrated B2B dashboard to track due dates. If you are a buyer, set up automated alerts before an invoice becomes due so you can schedule payments efficiently, protect your credit history, and take advantage of any early payment discounts. If you are a seller, configure automatic notifications for the day an invoice becomes past due. This flags delinquent accounts, letting your team pause new shipments and send payment reminders. For sellers: Establish a strict credit policy and stick to it When offering trade credit, protect your business from bad debt by providing clear policies. Establish explicit credit limits based on verified credit reports, charge transparent late fees or other such penalties for overdue accounts, and consider trade credit insurance. Trade credit FAQ What is an example of a trade credit? Imagine Company B orders $10,000 worth of blank T-shirts from a textile manufacturer to print graphics on them. Instead of demanding an upfront payment, the manufacturer ships the shirts immediately along with an invoice marked with net 30 terms. Company B receives the shirts, prints its designs, sells them to retail customers during the next two weeks, and uses that revenue to pay the $10,000 invoice to the manufacturer 28 days later. What are the advantages and disadvantages of trade credit? Using trade credit gives sellers a competitive advantage by helping to encourage customers to buy more, boosting sales volume and customer loyalty. For buyers, it functions as an interest-free loan that helps manage cash flow by avoiding upfront payment. However, buyers and sellers should consider the advantages and disadvantages. Buyers face late fees or a damaged credit rating if they miss payments, while sellers risk delayed revenue and bad debt if a buyer defaults on their open accounts. What are trade credits used for? Businesses use trade credit primarily to purchase physical inventory, buy raw manufacturing materials, or secure recurring corporate services without draining their cash reserves. It serves as short-term financing that bridges the time gap between buying goods from suppliers and collecting revenue from customers.

title: Construction Internet Speed Test: Is Your Connection Fast Enough? (August 2026)
summary: Run a construction internet speed test to see if your connection handles project management software, file uploads, and video calls. August 2026 guide.
body_text: You're paying for fast internet, but file uploads drag and video calls freeze mid-sentence. Before you call your ISP or blame the software, run a proper speed test from where your team actually works. The numbers you get back (download speed, upload speed, and latency) tell you exactly where the breakdown is happening and whether your connection can keep up with cloud-based tools, live collaboration, and the constant flow of jobsite data your projects depend on. TLDR: Run a speed test from your actual work location: 25 Mbps down/10 Mbps up handles small crews, but 50/25 Mbps works better for teams of 10-20 running full project management software. Upload speed matters more in construction than most realize . Field teams sending daily photos, submittals, and video calls need strong upload beyond download. High latency (over 100ms) kills video calls and makes cloud tools feel slow, even when your speed test looks fine. Metal framing and heavy equipment interfere with wireless signals on active sites. If apps lag but your speed test passes, the problem is likely your temporary network setup, not your ISP. Constructable caches drawings locally on mobile devices so crews can work through dead zones and sync automatically when connection returns. How to Run a Construction Internet Speed Test Running a test takes under a minute. Head to speedtest.net or fast.com , click go, and you'll get three numbers back. There are a few things worth knowing about each one before you read your results: Download speed measures how fast data comes to your device. This is what determines whether a 200-page drawing set loads in two seconds or two minutes. Upload speed measures how fast data leaves your device. Every photo you send, every RFI you submit, every large file you push out depends on this number. Ping measures how long a signal takes to make a round trip, in milliseconds. Low ping keeps apps feeling responsive. High ping makes everything feel sluggish, even when speeds look fine. Run the test from where you actually work—the job trailer, the tablet you carry on-site. A clean result from your office tells you nothing about what your superintendent is dealing with out in the field. Why Internet Speed Matters for Construction Projects Construction projects run on information. Drawings get updated; RFIs need answers before the crew goes idle; Submittals cycle through approvals; and video calls connect the trailer to the office daily. None of that holds together when the connection can't keep up. Many contractors cite communication between field and office as a major challenge, and spotty internet is often to blame. When a superintendent can't pull up a current drawing or a call keeps dropping mid-conversation, time gets lost and mistakes creep in. Cloud-based project management, large file transfers, and real-time collaboration all continuously drain your bandwidth. Your connection stopped being background infrastructure a long time ago. Understanding Download vs. Upload Speed Most internet plans are built for consumers who download far more than they upload. Streaming, browsing, loading pages. A typical residential package might offer 100 Mbps down and 10 Mbps up, and that works fine at home. Construction flips that assumption. Field teams send as much as they receive: daily log photos, video walkthroughs, submittal packages, inspection documentation. A superintendent uploading twenty jobsite photos from a morning walk puts real strain on that upload pipe. If your download looks fast but uploads crawl, you'll feel it in slow file submissions, choppy video calls, and photos that take forever to sync. Symmetrical speeds matter here more than most people realize. What Latency Means for Jobsite Communication Latency is the delay between sending a request and getting a response, measured in milliseconds. Under 50ms feels instant; over 100ms, you start noticing it. Push past 150ms on a video call and you're talking over each other, losing the thread entirely. Speed and latency are not the same thing. A fast connection with high latency still makes collaboration tools feel sluggish. Video calls freeze mid-sentence, shared documents feel like they're loading through wet cement, etc. For real-time field-to-office communication, that lag has real consequences. When a superintendent needs a quick PM call to resolve a drawing conflict before the crew stops work, high latency turns a two-minute answer into a ten-minute ordeal. Minimum Internet Speeds for Construction Software These numbers won't match every software vendor's spec sheet exactly, but they hold across most cloud-based construction tools. Think of them as a practical floor, not a ceiling. Scenario Min. Download Min. Upload Small crew (2-5 users), drawings and docs 25 Mbps 10 Mbps Mid-size team (10-20 users), full project management 50 Mbps 25 Mbps Large operation (20+ users), simultaneous video and file sync 100 Mbps 50 Mbps For a site with 20 people on video meetings at the same time, 50 Mbps of upload is the minimum worth targeting. Below that, someone's dropping off the call or waiting on a file that should have synced an hour ago. Common Connectivity Issues on Construction Sites A slow speed test result is not always the root problem. On active construction sites, connectivity issues often trace back to the environment before they trace back to the service plan. Common culprits worth checking: Metal framing and steel decking absorb and reflect wireless signals far more than wood or drywall Generators, compressors, and heavy equipment create electrical interference that disrupts wireless networks Temporary power drops and site-installed network hardware are rarely spec'd for continuous, high-bandwidth use Cellular signal is unreliable before permanent utilities are in, especially in below-grade or interior spaces If your speed test looks fine but apps still feel sluggish, suspect signal interference or your site's temporary network setup. Run a second test with a wired connection. If that number jumps, the issue is wireless. If both tests drag, look upstream at your ISP or temporary service plan. Wired vs. Wireless Connectivity Options Wired connections are the gold standard on a jobsite. A hardwired ethernet connection to your router or network switch gives you consistent speeds without the interference that kills wireless signals in steel-framed buildings or concrete structures. If you can run a cable, run a cable. That said, most trailers and field offices rely on wireless. Wi-Fi works fine if your router is close and the channel isn't congested. Cellular hotspots are common, too, especially on remote sites. LTE gets the job done for most tasks, while 5G handles heavier loads like large file transfers or video calls with the owner. Testing Your Connection Throughout the Project Set a baseline before work starts, when temporary internet first gets installed. Save those download, upload, and ping numbers somewhere you can actually find them. From there, retest after any network changes and before high-stakes activities like owner calls or large drawing transfers. When performance slips mid-project, that baseline is what tells you how far things have actually drifted. A Simple Testing Schedule Before mobilization, run a speed test on the day temporary internet goes live and record the results. Before any owner or architect video call, do a quick check so you are not caught off guard. After major network changes like a new router or ISP swap, retest to confirm you actually got what you paid for. Offline Functionality: When Internet Speed Doesn't Matter Not every field task requires a live connection—signal drops happen, remote sites exist, and cellular has limits that no speed test score can fix. Good construction software accounts for this reality. Some tools store drawings locally on your device, so plans stay accessible even when there's no signal. Once you're back online, activity syncs automatically without any manual effort from the team. Offline access covers the basics well: reviewing drawings, capturing notes, documenting conditions. For real-time collaboration or large file transfers, a solid connection still matters. But offline capability gives your crew a real cushion when the internet disappears mid-shift. How Constructable Works With Your Internet Connection Constructable is built for real jobsite conditions, not ideal ones. The iOS and Android apps keep drawing data cached locally, so your crew can work through a dead zone without stopping. Syncing occurs in the background once the connection is restored. The system stays responsive without requiring a strong signal for every action. Project data lives in the cloud but responds quickly even on a limited connection. Search pulls up specs, drawing details, or log entries fast, so a sluggish cellular signal on a remote site doesn't grind the workflow to a halt. Less time troubleshooting your connection means more time on the actual job. Final Thoughts on Checking Your Construction Internet Running a speed test from the trailer or tablet your crew uses tells you what your connection can really handle. Save those numbers, check them when performance drops, and know what to expect before a big call or file transfer goes out. Your tools should stay responsive even when bandwidth gets tight. If you want to talk through how Constructable handles spotty connections, reach out . FAQ Can I run a construction internet speed test on my phone or does it need to be from a computer? You can run it from any device—phone, tablet, or computer—but run the test from where you actually work. A speed test from your office desktop tells you nothing about what your superintendent is dealing with in the job trailer or on-site with a tablet. What's the minimum internet speed for construction project management software? For a small crew (2-5 users) working with drawings and documents, you need at least 25 Mbps download and 10 Mbps upload. If you have 10-20 users running full project management software, bump that to 50 Mbps down and 25 Mbps up. Larger operations with 20+ people on simultaneous video calls and file syncs should target 100 Mbps down and 50 Mbps up. Why does my upload speed matter more than download for jobsite work? Construction teams send as much data as they receive: daily log photos, video walkthroughs, submittal packages, inspection documentation all strain your upload pipe. A typical residential plan might give you 100 Mbps down and only 10 Mbps up, which works fine at home but crawls when a superintendent tries to upload 20 jobsite photos after a morning walk. Wired internet vs cellular hotspot for a job trailer? Wired ethernet is the gold standard if you can run a cable; you get consistent speeds without the interference that kills wireless signals in steel-framed buildings or concrete structures. Cellular hotspots work well on remote sites, with LTE handling most tasks and 5G managing heavier loads like large file transfers or owner video calls. Can construction software work without internet on a jobsite? Yes, if it's built for offline use. Good construction software stores drawings locally on your device so plans stay accessible when the signal drops, then syncs automatically once you're back online. Offline capability covers reviewing drawings, capturing notes, and documenting conditions; real-time collaboration and large file transfers still require a solid connection.

title: How to Roll Through International Roadcheck with Confidence, Ease, and Extra Cash!
body_text: This year's International Roadcheck will take place between May 17-19, 2022 and focus on wheel ends. The Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA) organizes an annual International Roadcheck , which they define as "a 72-hour high-visibility, high-volume commercial motor vehicle inspection" enforcement and educational initiative across North America. Last year, there were 40,000 inspections throughout the three inspection days. There were 19,786 Level I Inspections in the U.S. specifically, resulting in 4,136 vehicles and 1,083 driver out-of-service orders . Whether you have your authority or are leased onto another, it's a critical time for Owner-Operators. With a good attitude and proper preparation, you can treat the days of International Roadcheck as you would any other on the road - ones in which you prioritize the safety and well-being of yourself and others. Many carriers, like TrueNorth, give bonuses for clean inspections. Let's look at what to expect during International Roadcheck and six proactive steps you can take to prepare and roll through it with confidence, ease, and did we mention - extra cash!? What to Expect Between May 17-19, 2022, CVSA-certified inspectors will conduct North American Standard Inspections on all commercial vehicles, which of course, includes trucks. Throughout the three days, vehicle, driver, and cargo inspections take place all over roadways - from roadsides to weigh and inspection stations to temporary inspection sites. You may receive any level of inspection during International Roadcheck. Level I is the most comprehensive and consists of reviewing the driver‚Äôs paperwork and a complete inspection of the vehicle. It‚Äôs a process that can take up to 60 minutes to complete. The following is subject to inspection: Paperwork: Commercial Driver's License (CDL) Medical Examiner's Certificate Skill Performance Evaluation (SPE) Certificate (if applicable) Alcohol and drugs Driver's record of duty status Hours of service Vehicle inspection report(s) Physical: Seat belt Brake systems Cargo securement Coupling devices Driveline/driveshaft Electrical cables and systems in engine and battery compartments Exhaust systems Frames Fuel systems Lighting devices (headlamps, tail lamps, stop lamps, turn signals and lamps/flags on projecting loads) Steering mechanisms Suspensions Tires Van and open-top trailer bodies Wheels, rims and hubs Windshield wipers Level II requires the paperwork portion of the Level 1 plus a visual (walk-around) of the equipment and Level III is a driver-only (paperwork) inspection. You will likely receive a CVSA decal for your vehicle if you pass an inspection. The decal is valid for three months and signals to inspectors that your vehicle and driver passed the inspection, reducing the likelihood that you are subjected to another while it's valid, unless a violation occurs. Like any roadside inspection, if you receive any violations during your inspection, you receive points that stay on both your carrier‚Äôs CSA score and your individual PSP score. You may receive an out-of-service (OOS) order for any critical violations found, which prevents you from operating as the driver or vehicle until you resolve the violation(s). Focus on Wheel Ends While all vehicle, driver, and cargo components are subject to inspection, this year's wheel ends are a priority due to their frequency of violations. Wheel separations are a common cause of accidents. In years past, wheel ends violations have accounted for roughly one-quarter of vehicle out-of-service (OOS) violations during International Roadcheck. This year, we can reduce the high safety risk that wheel end failures pose by bringing wheel ends into focus. In particular, the wheel-end inspection includes "wheels and rims, wheel fasteners (hub and lug nuts), wheel seals and leaks, and tires (tread depth, condition, inflation, leaks, in contact with the vehicle)." Your hubs must all be in good working condition to prevent damage such as a leak, where oil can move around the wheels, get into braking components, and even catch on fire. To learn more about wheel ends, this 1-minute video is for you. How to Prepare Whether you're leased onto a carrier or running your own authority, give yourself enough runway to adequately prepare for International Roadcheck. Below is a checklist you can follow to do everything possible for a clean inspection. 1. Familiarize Yourself with Inspections Staying aware of what inspectors are looking for and what will be required of you as the Owner-Operator is the first step. The CVSA's North American Standard Roadside Inspection Vehicle Cheat Sheet is a useful guide to what to expect during the inspection. In addition, our Owner-Operators Only article, CVSA Inspections: Understanding and Preparing for Them , walks you through what exactly is included in each level - within both the paperwork and physical categories. 2. Ensure Up-to-date Maintenance If your truck or trucks undergo regular maintenance by qualified technicians, you're on your way to setting yourself up for success to pass an inspection. If you have not kept up with regular maintenance, getting your truck to a shop as quickly as possible is important. One way to take your preparation to the next level and ensure everything is in full working condition is to get a complete Federal Annual DOT inspection from a reputable vendor for both the truck and the trailer. Remind technicians and mechanics to explain what inspectors look for and pay particular attention to wheel ends for loose fasteners, stretched studs, cracks, proper torque of fasteners, axle seals for leaks, tire inflation, and tread depth, cuts, or other damage to tires. Having a fresh inspection sticker on both pieces of equipment doesn't guarantee anything, but it can help. 3. Be Diligent about Pre- and Post-Trip Inspections Even with regular maintenance, a critical violation could occur any day. The requirement to complete the daily pre- and post-trip inspections is essential. While many drivers rush through it or even fail to do it, keeping up with these daily inspections can help reveal the discovery of potential safety issues or mechanical problems that could prevent you from having a bad inspection or worse, a dangerous event on the road. Want a refresher on how to do your pre-trip? Watch this ultimate video guide! 4. Pay Attention to Presentation It always helps when your equipment is fresh and clean. Pay extra for the tire shine at the Blue Beacon. Replace faded/torn reflective tape, lug nut covers, mudflaps, etc. Invest in some brake cleaner and clean up the pads so the original color and any other critical brake parts show through. Double-check your permit book to be sure everything is current and you have a neat and orderly permit book to present if needed (including required supplementary ELD items). Make sure you look professional and presentable. While these things do not guarantee you will pass the inspection, they may increase your chances. 5. Expect to be Inspected You have a high chance of being inspected during International Roadcheck. Don't assume that it won‚Äôt happen to you. Always stay diligent, organized, and prepared for the greatest chance of passing. 6. Bring a Positive Attitude and a Smile It‚Äôs important to remember that while inspectors fulfill their responsibility to inspect, they're also human. And just as you would expect anyone to treat you with dignity and respect, they expect the same of you. A positive attitude and a smile go a long way. Why Inspections Matter Every carrier with a Department of Transportation (DOT) number receives an ongoing and updated safety score as part of the Compliance, Safety, Accountability (CSA) program. Essentially, your CSA score is indicative of your business success as a carrier, impacting the way drivers, inspectors, shippers, receivers, brokers, and more, interact with you. Through a ranking system called Behavior Analysis and Safety Improvement Categories (BASIC) scores, each fleet receives scores for 7 categories every month: Unsafe Driving, Driver Fitness, Hours-of-service Compliance, Vehicle Maintenance, Controlled Substances, Crash Indicator, and Hazardous Materials Compliance. With any inspection, you're at risk of receiving a violation, which adds points to your score. The fewer points you have, the better. And because there is only one score per fleet, within each BASIC category, each driver‚Äôs individual actions or inactions impact the whole. We take an in-depth look at this concept in our article Why CSA Scores Should Be Treated Like a Team Sport . How do CSAs scores impact International Roadcheck? Carriers with higher (poorer) scores are subject to increased roadside inspections, presenting an additional risk to the health of your business through delays and limited opportunities. Final Thoughts International Roadcheck does not have to feel like a burden but rather an opportunity for increased safety and wellbeing on our roadways. As an Owner-Operator, you work diligently on the success of your business, including every safety measure. International Roadcheck provides an opportunity to prove you're following all possible safety protocols, share pride and joy in your equipment, and earn some extra money through a bonus. Remember, Roadcheck is not just enforcement; it's an educational tool for improvement - for the safety and wellbeing of all. We are confident that you can and will pass inspections with flying colors. And we can't wait to celebrate with you once you do! Other relevant articles: DVIR: Pre-Trip and Post-Trip Inspections CVSA Inspections: Understanding and Preparing for Them Why CSA Scores Should Be Treated Like a Team Sport
